questions.prompt: State the charge of an up quark in units of \(e\).
questions.answer: An up quark has charge \(+2/3\).

questions.prompt: State the charge of a down quark in units of \(e\).
questions.answer: A down quark has charge \(-1/3\).

questions.prompt: What particle mediates the strong interaction between quarks?
questions.answer: The gluon mediates the strong interaction between quarks.

questions.prompt: Find the charge of \(uud\).
questions.answer:
\[
Q=+\frac23+\frac23-\frac13=+1
\]
So \(uud\) has charge \(+e\).

questions.prompt: Find the charge of \(udd\).
questions.answer:
\[
Q=+\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0
\]
So \(udd\) is neutral.

questions.prompt: What is colour charge?
questions.answer: Colour charge is the type of charge associated with the strong interaction. Quarks carry colour charge and gluons interact with colour charge.

questions.prompt: Why are free isolated quarks not observed?
questions.answer: The strong interaction confines quarks inside colour-neutral hadrons. Trying to separate quarks produces new hadrons rather than isolated quarks.

questions.prompt: Find the charge of a \(u\bar s\) meson.
questions.answer: A \(u\) quark has charge \(+2/3\). An anti-strange quark has charge \(+1/3\). The total is \(+1\).

questions.prompt: What is the baryon number of one quark and one antiquark?
questions.answer: A quark has \(B=+1/3\). An antiquark has \(B=-1/3\). Together they have net baryon number \(0\).

questions.prompt: Why must observable hadrons be colour neutral?
questions.answer: Confinement means isolated colour charge is not observed. Quarks combine as colour-neutral baryons or mesons.

questions.prompt: Find the charge and baryon number of \(sss\).
questions.answer: Each strange quark has charge \(-1/3\), so the total charge is \(-1\). Three quarks give baryon number \(+1\).

questions.prompt: Find the charge of \(d\bar u\).
questions.answer: The \(d\) quark has charge \(-1/3\). The anti-up quark has charge \(-2/3\). The total charge is \(-1\).

questions.prompt: Explain why a proton and neutron have similar masses despite different charge.
questions.answer: Both are baryons made from three light quarks and most of their mass comes from strong-interaction energy, not simply from quark rest masses or electric charge.

questions.prompt: Why are gluons different from photons in the way they interact with their own field?
questions.answer: Gluons carry colour charge, so they can interact with other gluons. Photons do not carry electric charge, so ordinary electromagnetic field self-interaction is absent at this level.

questions.prompt: A hadron has baryon number \(+1\), charge \(0\), and contains only up and down quarks. Identify a likely quark content.
questions.answer: A likely quark content is \(udd\), the neutron. It has baryon number \(+1\) and charge \(+2/3-1/3-1/3=0\).

questions.prompt: Use quark content to explain the charge conservation in \(n\to p+e^-+\bar\nu_e\).
questions.answer: The neutron is \(udd\) and the proton is \(uud\). A down quark effectively changes to an up quark, increasing hadron charge by \(+1\). The emitted electron has charge \(-1\), so total charge remains zero.

questions.prompt: A meson has quark content \(s\bar u\). Find its charge and baryon number.
questions.answer: The strange quark has charge \(-1/3\), and the anti-up quark has charge \(-2/3\), giving total charge \(-1\). The baryon number is \(+1/3-1/3=0\).

questions.prompt: Why does adding energy to separate quarks produce jets of hadrons in high-energy collisions?
questions.answer: The colour field energy grows as quarks separate. At high enough energy, new quark-antiquark pairs form, producing streams of colour-neutral hadrons rather than isolated quarks.

questions.prompt: Explain why a \(qq\) two-quark state is not an ordinary observed meson or baryon.
questions.answer: A meson is \(q\bar q\) and a baryon is \(qqq\). A two-quark \(qq\) state is not one of the standard colour-neutral hadron combinations in this introductory model.

questions.prompt: How do fractional quark charges still produce integer hadron charges in common hadrons?
questions.answer: Allowed quark combinations add fractional charges in groups such as \(qqq\) or \(q\bar q\). The sums for common isolated hadrons are integer multiples of \(e\), such as \(+1\), \(0\), or \(-1\).
